enonce_markdown: A constant force $\mathbf F=(3\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-2\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ moves its point of application through the displacement $\mathbf d=(2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+5\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$. The work done by the force is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For a constant force, the work done is the scalar product $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d$ of the force and the displacement; it is negative when the force has a component opposite to the motion.

### Solution

$$W=(3)(2)+(4)(-1)+(-2)(5)=6-4-10=-8\ \mathrm J.$$

The value $12$ comes from treating the $\mathbf k$ product as $+10$, and $2$ from omitting the $\mathbf k$ components; $8$ ignores the sign of the result.

**Answer: A.**

enonce_markdown: A trader at a market in Douala drags a crate along a horizontal floor by a rope. The tension in the rope is $150\ \mathrm N$ and the rope makes an angle of $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. The crate moves $12\ \mathrm m$. The work done by the tension is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For a constant force $F$ and displacement $s$ at an angle $\alpha$ to the force, $W=Fs\cos\alpha$: only the component of the force along the displacement does work.

### Solution

$$W=150\times12\times\cos30^\circ=1800\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=900\sqrt3\approx1559\ \mathrm J.$$

The value $1800$ ignores the angle; $900$ uses $\sin30^\circ$ instead of $\cos30^\circ$; $278$ comes from a calculator set to radians.

**Answer: D.**

enonce_markdown: A load of mass $40\ \mathrm{kg}$ is raised at constant speed up a smooth slope, by a force acting parallel to the slope. The slope is $6\ \mathrm m$ long and inclined at $20^\circ$ to the horizontal. Taking $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the work done by the force is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

At constant speed the resultant force along the slope is zero, so the applied force equals the component of the weight down the slope, $mg\sin\alpha$. Work done $=$ force $\times$ distance along the slope.

### Solution

$$W=mg\sin20^\circ\times6=40\times9.8\times0.3420\times6\approx804.4\ \mathrm J.$$

Using $\cos20^\circ$ gives $2210.2$; ignoring the slope angle gives $2352.0$; forgetting $g$ gives $82.1$.

**Answer: B.**

enonce_markdown: A particle moves along the $x$-axis under a force $F=(4x+3)\ \mathrm N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x$, where $x$ is in metres. The work done by the force as the particle moves from $x=1$ to $x=4$ is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

When the force varies with position, the work done is $W=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}F\,dx$. Do not multiply the force at one end by the distance.

### Solution

$$W=\int_1^4(4x+3)\,dx=\Bigl[2x^2+3x\Bigr]_1^4=(32+12)-(2+3)=39\ \mathrm J.$$

The value $21$ is $F(1)\times3$, $57$ is $F(4)\times3$, and $44$ forgets to subtract the value at $x=1$.

**Answer: C.**

enonce_markdown: An elastic string has natural length $0.8\ \mathrm m$ and modulus of elasticity $120\ \mathrm N$. Find the work that must be done to stretch the string from a length of $0.9\ \mathrm m$ to a length of $1.2\ \mathrm m$.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For an elastic string with extension $x$, the tension is $T=\dfrac{\lambda x}{l}$. The work done in stretching it from extension $x_1$ to $x_2$ is $\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\frac{\lambda x}{l}\,dx=\frac{\lambda}{2l}\left(x_2^2-x_1^2\right)$, the change in elastic potential energy.

### Solution

The extensions are $x_1=0.9-0.8=0.1\ \mathrm m$ and $x_2=1.2-0.8=0.4\ \mathrm m$ (not the lengths themselves).

$$W=\frac{120}{2(0.8)}\left(0.4^2-0.1^2\right)=75\,(0.16-0.01)=75\times0.15=11.25\ \mathrm J.$$

enonce_markdown:
A block of mass $5\ \mathrm{kg}$ is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at $25^\circ$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $0.2$. Take $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

By calculating the work done by each force, find the speed of the block after it has slid $8\ \mathrm m$ down the plane.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Work--energy principle: the total work done by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy. The normal reaction does no work (it is perpendicular to the motion); gravity does positive work $mg\sin\alpha\times s$ down the slope; friction $\mu R$ does negative work.

### Solution

Perpendicular to the plane there is no acceleration, so $R=mg\cos25^\circ=5\times9.8\times\cos25^\circ\approx44.41\ \mathrm N$ and the friction force is $\mu R\approx8.88\ \mathrm N$.

Work done by gravity (component down the slope): $5\times9.8\times\sin25^\circ\times8\approx165.67\ \mathrm J$.

Work done by friction: $-8.88\times8\approx-71.05\ \mathrm J$.

Work done by $R$: $0$.

Net work $\approx94.61\ \mathrm J$, equal to the gain in kinetic energy from rest:

$$\tfrac12(5)v^2=94.61\ \Rightarrow\ v^2\approx37.85\ \Rightarrow\ v\approx6.15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$
